en: Chagatai was to fight,
They were to contend and dig for the people,
A spear of steel would be made,
Thrusting the spear and striking the host,
They would take the road from across the world,
They would mount their tulpar steeds,
Mounting tulpars, they would seize the banner,
Rejoicing in the one who was born,
Allowing no enemy to approach,
Setting the fortress defenders’ hearts aflame,
Mounting him at the true place,
Dressing him in a shield for truth,
Becoming like a great fortress,
Becoming one who had stood there before,
This struggle would be wondrous,
He took a spear as large as a pestle.
He bound them so none could move,
He again threw the enemy into disorder,
When wrath was granted, he wheeled about.
When the one he met became venomous,
The matter wove itself,
Putting on a black coat,
From the hardship that watched the ravine,
He struck against the enemy,
Driving his champion elsewhere,
One who had thrust forward before,
Who had ever seen such a crimson figure?
A red sun from the ring-bearing lord,
His manner and gait were unlike others,
Gripping his spear, he tensed,
His blue trousers were wrapped close,
At the cry of conflict he sprang up,
Showing his warrior nature,
Swaying like a contrary tempest,
If a thousand fell in the night,
When his brow entered trouble,
Even if all stopped mounting,
They dressed him in an iron coat,
They mounted him on Sai-Kuman,
One who had pushed forward before,
Who had ever seen such a crimson figure?
When the blue eagle observed,
He mounted the tulpar granted by Tengir,
Binding the condition that allowed no delay,
His charge flew like a cloud,
Seeing the enemy, the people turned again,
As though the Creator had made it so,
His stallion moved as if plucking strings.
The dark-red colt was a living force,
He alone rode the camel.
Toward the snare cast across the mountain,
The gathered peoples split apart.
Its mane and tail were finely formed,
It raced as swiftly as an arrow,
It seemed to gaze halfway up the sky,
Though well-fed, it never lost its discipline,
Each bound carried it a full stride,
It made the tamarisk-lined slope tremble,
For a brave and valiant warrior,
It was fit for the road he would ride.
Let us take up the tale handed down from long ago,
The tale of one who shook Ala-Too,
Whose swift horse stood ready at the tethering line,
A narrow-hearted, shallow soul,
Who routed a mass of four thousand,
Who cried “Let fate decide!” and flew into the gunfire,
Against the wrathful infidels,
Who leveled his spear toward Khan-Too,
Who gave his precious life for his people,
Willing to offer it in sacrifice,
Without flinching or weakening his arm,
He stood firm at the very foot of the assault,
The wrathful thousand stood grim before him,
The women sat there in alarm,
Though dark blood flowed through the ravine,
Though tormented, he never lost the power of speech,
His face was wrinkled, his venom spent,
Such were the deeds he did when he charged,
Where is the hero Kenen now?
He had been one among the heroes.
He broke through the enemy line and opened a road,
When arrows poured down like rain,
When bullets fell like a hailstorm,
When blood was spilled and people fell,
Whenever he met a furious foe,
He faced him head-on and stood his ground,
Firing his gun and drawing his bow,
He fought without flinching,
He was a peerless hero.
Oil flowed from his fingers,
Blood flowed from his nails,
He never strayed from his purpose,
Rich treasure and abundance emerged,
Blood flowed from what he drew,
A soul arose to return,
He alone drew the enemy against him.
If it was a moonless night,
If it was a day when sight was veiled,
Later he would not stumble in speech.
Once in moonless darkness,
On the side where Mana lay,
He was one among the marksmen.
He won fame with the spear,
Among masters who found a stratagem against the enemy,
Among heroes complete in cunning,
Among warriors skilled in wisdom,
He was one of the crafty men.
When he turned, he was worth a thousand souls,
The lion Kenen became khan,
He was a hero weighty as a mountain,
He won fame against a thousand in battle,
He was a hero of hard conflict,
The heroes traveled day after day,
Traveling among thousands without taking a horse,
He lay in Blue Kashgar,
Following Kayyp’s road to the left,
Joining Ala-Too to him,
Driving them onward behind him,
Safely through many nights,
He traveled the shadowed road by his own will,
Urging on his dappled horse,
Crossing the ridges with a roar,
His solitary horse granted by Tengir.
The grey-haired elder said this with force,
With a roar as though the earth had split,
A tumult rose to the heavens,
The many-colored host divided,
They met in a standing battle,
The warriors of the five passes,
Charged together and struck,
Manas at their head, Khan Shayköö,
They struck by the grave mound,
They drove straight ahead with a rush,
Of the radiant elder Manas,
It was told concerning the grave mound,
There were two wings of the enveloping host,
Before them stood Kenen’s mighty claim,
All of them were heroes,
Ebegey and Köböy, your two elders,
The hero Jeljetpes joined them as a companion,
They swept through the whole army,
Like a fat barren mare’s colt,
They laid them waste in torment,
Horses came by tens from the right,
They formed troops of ten,
In their midst stood the dear Kazakh,
His neck worn and wasted,
If the horse supports him, let it be tethered,
Your white axe tucked beneath your arm,
Your valiant hero appeared,
He had only just taken it in hand.
Ebegey and Köböy, the two lions,
At hero Kenen’s side,
Speaking softly, they began their counsel,
Ebegey and Köböy began to speak,
Hero Kenen, lend your ear,
You must understand one thing,
In the end you will stand firm.
Without delay, this affair fell apart,
His enemies multiplied,
Have we been left bewildered and without recourse?
The condition of the Kyrgyz became plain,
This wretched old Tekeche,
His oppressive nature became clear.
What good is there in blood being shed?
Countless troubles came into view.
Ah, taking command through cunning,
He still possessed the prestige to seize power,
That noble one was Kenen’s son.
He had occupied two lands,
From of old the Chinese had been foes,
As for Ala-Too and the Kyrgyz,
Few remained who could become a people.
Ebegey and wise Kongoy,
I saw Chargyn from afar,
This was precious through all the ages,
Nothing like it could be found on earth,
Of this accursed swine,
If any Kyrgyz fell into his hands,
There seemed no end to what he did.
This land where our cord was cut and our swaddling washed,
This Ala-Too our forefathers tended,
Its true state upon the earth could no longer be seen,
Life would not be set right,
The people who had lived in freedom,
He would not let the people settle in their summer pastures,
He plundered their sustenance and ruined them,
Our lot in this place would not improve.
For this wretch, half the people would spill their blood,
This land would come under his heel,
The people and land of this Kakan remained behind,
His boastful tongue was backed by brute force,
A man must rise to stand against him.
Can a surrounded man prosper?
O dear people, lofty as a mountain,
What course could we take?
Now the enemy is coming,
What remedy could there be?
We have not the strength to fight,
Take heed of what you have been told,
Lion Kenen, heed your words,
I shall turn away from wrath,
Know it, if you agree to these words,
Like the Kyrgyz amid the teeming multitude,
Know that I am one of your people here,
The torment of anger,
Know that you will depart unharmed if you consent.
Ebegey and Köböy said this,
And, having spoken, drew their words to a close,
Hero Jeljetpes then said this,
Look outside, wolf-eyed one,
My enemies will fall and drink blood,
Is the open field my hero's battleground?
Without blood being spilled in that hour,
Without the great conflict becoming famed,
Will he then set about fighting?
If he bows his head before the warriors,
Will all good fortune not depart?
The spirited thoroughbred racer,
The brave man headed by a khan,
Will he not die and pass away in regret?
Let us strike that bristling swine,
Will the fox not catch him in the end?
If an unconquered people bows its head,
Will it not shrink today from what it sees?
Will it not draw near to witness it?
Will it not say that its heart is with me?
He chose his warriors and launched the attack,
Would he not unleash the valiant Kyrgyz?
Would he not cut down whoever resisted?
Would he not send forth warriors sharp as swords?
If one fell into his hands, would he let him go?
Would he not slaughter those seeking protection?
Would he not consume even their mutton?
No trembling khan remained,
Would he not strip the people bare?
Not merely your livestock, but your head,
Would he not make it an object of cruel sport?
What your treasury had yielded,
Would he not seize it before all the world?
Would he not strike anyone who faced him?
His forefather was Aleke,
After him came the warrior Kancha,
Would he not exact blood-price from the Bulgars?
The Kyrgyz cannot attain your vengeance,
Can the small Kyrgyz people not recover?
“Indeed, father, here it is,” he said,
Would he forget the heroes?
Would he not bring down whoever confronted him?
So he spoke of a feud whose end none could reach,
The black host came once again,
Many binding words poured forth,
He told the tale through to its end.
When the warrior Kenen heard this,
His soul boiled like flame,
At the depraved Chinese swine,
